projects.project_name: Strengthening Health Infrastructure for Livestock Disease Control
projects.impagency: Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying
projects.project_abstract: 1. Introduction: The Government of India is focusing on strengthening the core capacity of animal health system in India, including upgrading existing veterinary infrastructure such as diagnostic laboratories and facilities, veterinary hospitals and dispensaries, strengthening surveillance and disease reporting capacity, building capacity at community level and One Health coordination capacity. Strengthening Health Infrastructure for Livestock Disease Control Program (SHIELD) will be a subset of the larger government program and contribute to the overarching government Livestock Disease Control program (LHDCP) and will be implemented by the Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying for over five years (2026-2031) as a 100 percent centrally sponsored national program. The overall LHDCP size is US$1.3 billion, of which the SHIELD Program boundary is US$162 million, to which the PforR will contribute US$81.123 million.2. Government Program: The DAHD is implementing an overarching animal health management program, namely the Livestock Health and Disease Control Program (LHDCP) for the period 2026-2031. The key objectives of the LHDCP are to maintain a healthy, disease-free livestock population, and control animal diseases including zoonotic diseases. The program contributes directly to India’s Viksit Bharat agenda through its contribution to farmer incomes, employment generation and entrepreneurship by improving animal health, and increasing livestock productivity and production. In addition, controlling zoonoses and increasing the capacity of disease management directly contributes to reducing the threat of future pandemics and related shocks. 3. The program consists of the following components (i) Critical Animal Disease Control Programme (CADCP) to control of Classical Swine Fever and Peste des Petits Ruminants; (ii) Establishment and Strengthening of Veterinary Hospitals, Dispensaries and Mobile Veterinary Units (ESVHD) to support operationalizations of Mobile Veterinary Units; (iii) Assistance to States for Control of Animal Diseases (ASCAD) that support surveillance and monitoring support important livestock and poultry diseases, vaccination of economically important animal diseases (livestock and poultry), control of emerging and exotic diseases, strengthening the Veterinary Council of India; (iv) National Animal Disease Control Programme (NADCP) to support vaccination against priority livestock such as Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD), Brucellosis, Classica Swine Fever (CSF) and Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR), and (v) National Digital Livestock Mission (NDLM) to support disease reporting, surveillance and (vi) Programme for Strengthening Health Infrastructure for Livestock Disease Control (SHIELD) focusing on improving district and state diagnostic facilities, block level veterinary hospitals and capacity building of veterinary institutions (to which World Bank SHIELD project will contribute).4. The government program has achieved significant results. Achievements include the vaccination of 1,391.72 million vaccinations against FMD covering around 316.5 million animals and the declaration of FMD-free zones in three states; immunization against other economically important diseases (Brucellosis, PPR, CSF and Lumpy Skin Diseases), and the initiation of a control program for classical swine fever in the northeastern regions. However, these achievements are constrained by various factors including poor diagnostic and surveillance capacity, veterinary human resource shortfall, poor disease reporting and surveillance, insufficient investment at community level to improve disease reporting and risks management. 5. The proposed PforR aims to support the government in implementing selected elements of the LHDCP, focusing on building system capacity for animal health management in an integrated, outcome-focused manner, as well as using a decentralized approach to strengthen disease surveillance at community level, enabling early disease detection, containment and strengthening the livestock economy. The Program will support subsets of the ASCAD, NDLM and SHIELD, and other areas of support will be refined during program preparation. In particular, the PforR will focus on strengthening the core capacity of animal health management, strengthen critical surveillance infrastructure, support community level awareness and training of veterinary professionals in all States and UTs to better prevent, detect and control animal disease outbreaks.6. The indicative expenditure framework for the overarching LHDCP government program (p”) for fiscal years 2026 to 2031 is US$1.3 billion. The Program (“P”), which forms part of the broader government program (“p”), has a defined expenditure boundary estimated at US$162 million over five years. Of this amount, the World Bank will provide US$81.123 million in financing, accounting for 50 percent of the program’s total budget. The Bank-supported PforR Program focuses on institutional capacity building, systems development to enhance disease diagnostic and surveillance, improving the quality and coverage of diagnostic and veterinary services and investment at community level for increasing awareness on good practices, disease reporting, risk management and One Health coordination. The PforR Program will exclude civil works related to the construction of new facilities, and procurement of vaccines. Civil works under the Program will include renovations and upgrading of existing physical infrastructure (e.g., veterinary hospitals, veterinary dispensaries, laboratories).7. CPF Alignment: The proposed Program aligns directly with the India Country Partnership Framework (FY26–31) through the following outcome areas: (1) Rural Resilience and Prosperity and Investing in People for Jobs-ready Workforce.  It contributes to CPF Outcome 1 on “Fostering prosperity and resilience for better opportunities in rural areas” through improving (i) infrastructure of veterinary services and diagnostic infrastructure critical to animal disease management and prevention which contributes to livestock production and productivity; (ii) supporting digital innovations to veterinary services and advisory service delivery, especially for rural households in remote areas. In addition, through (2) Outcome 3 on “Investing in people, for job ready workforce” through upgrading skills and strengthening health”. The program will support training and upskilling of livestock farmers on good animal husbandry practices, staff of identified livestock points (including livestock markets and abattoirs) on good handling practices, to improve biosecurity measures to reduce disease risks and improve livestock productivity.  In addition, the program will invest in the training and upskilling of para-veterinarians, laboratory personnel, field staff including forest department staff and livestock community extension workers. At the macro level these improvements can help increase livestock trade and improve access to disease-free animal protein.8. Jobs and Public Health: Livestock is one of India's largest rural employment generators. More than 70 percent of rural households derive some livelihood benefit from livestock, with the dairy sector alone engaging over 80 million farmers. The sector offers a major pathway for job creation, women's economic empowerment, income diversification, and rural transformation. Animal disease outbreaks can have far-reaching economic consequences beyond the livestock sector, specifically by disrupting agriculture, food processing, hospitality and manufacturing, among other sectors. Indirect costs, which are often overlooked, account for nearly half of the total losses, justifying greater public investment in disease prevention. The public health burden of zoonotic diseases can be enormous. Brucellosis, a zoonotic animal disease, is estimated to cause 11.7 Disability Adjusted Life Years (DALY) per 100,000 people, disproportionately affecting r

projects.project_name: K-BREEZE: Karnataka Bus Reforms for Efficiency, Electrification & Sustainability Operation
projects.impagency: Transport Department, State Government of Karnataka
projects.project_abstract: (1) Context and Key IssuesKarnataka, India’s ninth most populous state (69 million in 2026), and has above-average urbanization (38.7%), with urban growth highly concentrated in major centers, most notably in the State capital- Bengaluru.  Private vehicle growth—particularly cars and two-wheelers at ~10%—has outpaced state-owned bus services, which expanded at only ~2% Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR). This divergence has created a widening gap between demand and formal public transport supply. The three regional RTCs - Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC), Northwestern Karnataka Road Transport Corporation (NWKRTC), and Kalyana Karnataka Road Transport Corporation (KKRTC) operate about 19,000 buses serving rural, semi-urban and intercity/ interstate routes, whereas in Bengaluru, the Bengaluru Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC), urban RTC operates 7,000 buses. Buses account for 41% of all non-agricultural work trips and are particularly critical for women and low-income populations. However:• Access gaps persist in rural areas, with many villages lacking direct bus connectivity.• Urban congestion and emissions are rising due to rapid motorization, increasing travel times and costs. The challenge extends beyond fleet size to fleet composition and modernization:• Electric bus (e-bus) adoption is concentrated in Bengaluru (~25% of fleet), with minimal uptake in other regions.• Depot and charging infrastructure remain inadequate, and RTCs lack technical capacity for e-bus system management.• Shift to Gross Cost Contracts (GCC) requires RTCs to transition from operators to performance-oriented contract managers. Financial and institutional constraints have compounded these issues:• High input costs, below cost recovery fares, operational inefficiencies, and COVID-19 impacts have led to accumulated losses and declining creditworthiness.• RTCs rely on discretionary state support, limiting access to commercial finance and private sector participation.• Fragmented institutional systems and weak data integration hinder route rationalization, service optimization, and demand-responsive planning. (2) Program DescriptionIn 2022, the Government of Karnataka (GoK) adopted a strategic roadmap to transform RTCs into financially sustainable and operationally efficient public transport providers, identifying 21 reform areas. The program is anchored on three pillars:1. Improving operational efficiency and financial sustainability2. Expanding urban and regional bus services (with ~50% private participation)3. Strengthening institutional frameworks and capacity The proposed Karnataka Bus Reforms for Efficiency, Electrification & Sustainability (K-BREEZE) PforR operation supports a targeted subset of activities aligned with this roadmap, organized around three interrelated results areas (RAs):• Improving operational efficiency and financial sustainability of RTCs  o Introduce a performance-linked financial architecture, replacing ad hoc subsidies with Public Transport Service Contracts (PTSCs)  o Establish transparent fare revision mechanisms to improve cost recovery and fiscal predictability • Creating and Enabling Ecosystem for Private Sector Participation in Bus Service Delivery   o Develop bankable contractual frameworks through standardized GCCs supported by a Liquidity Support Facility (LSF)  o Improve risk allocation to enable private operators and lenders to scale investments in fleet expansion, especially e-buses  o Expand depot and charging infrastructure to enable fleet electrification • Institutional strengthening and capacity building:  o Support RTCs’ transition from fleet operators to professional contract managers  o Upgrade technical capabilities, digital systems, and planning functions(3) Strategic AlignmentK-BREEZE is closely aligned with the India Country Partnership Framework (CPF) FY2026–2031 and the Government’s Viksit Bharat 2047 vision.The operation supports private sector led job creation:• Generate ~40,000 direct and indirect jobs across operations, manufacturing, and services• Create significant opportunities for private operators, lenders, and International Finance Corporation (IFC) - World Bank Group's private sector lending arm. IFC can mobilize large scale debt and equity capital into the bus market, as this operation would create enabling ecosystem for private sector participation through improving contractual bankability and creditworthiness. • Mobilize large-scale investment into sustainable mobilityIt directly contributes to the CPF outcomes:• Outcome 1: Rural Prosperity and Resilience  o Expands bus connectivity to underserved villages  o Improves access to jobs and markets, boosting local economic activity • Outcome 2: Urban Development  o Enhances urban mobility through scaled private investment  o Improves air quality and reduces congestion  o Strengthens Bengaluru’s role as an economic growth hub • Outcome 3: Investing in People  o Builds a job-ready workforce through institutionalized skill development  o Supports workforce transition to new technologies and service models The operation is designed under the CPF’s “Budget-Plus” and “Finance-Plus” approaches:• Catalyzing private capital through Public Private Partnerships (PPPs)• Combining financing with global knowledge, digitalization, and skill development• Driving system-wide transformation rather than incremental improvements  It also aligns with the WBG Climate Change Action Plan by promoting low-emission transport (e-buses) and supporting climate mitigation and adaptation outcomes.
projects.pdo: To improve access to sustainable public transport services in Karnataka, leveraging private sector participation.

projects.major_sector_name: Financial Sector,Industry, Trade and Services,Public Administration,Social Protection
projects.project_abstract: The development objective of the Boosting Job Creation in the Private Sector Development Policy Financing for India program is to promote private sector–led job creation by improving the business environment, enhancing trade and investment openness, and mobilizing private capital to support firm growth. Aligned with Government priorities and the World Bank Group Country Partnership Framework for India FY26–31 under the Viksit Bharat @2047 vision, the program supports reforms that reduce regulatory and compliance costs, minimize business risks, expand access to markets and finance, and create enabling conditions for firms to grow and generate more and better jobs. It builds on sustained policy dialogue, analytical work, and ongoing World Bank Group engagements in areas such as MSME finance, trade, competitiveness, and financial sector development. The operation also advances the Maximizing Finance for Development approach by addressing regulatory, legal, and financial constraints to private investment and is aligned with the goals of the Paris Agreement on mitigation and adaptation.
projects.pdo: Boosting job creation in the private sector by improving the business environment, opening markets to trade and investment, and leveraging private capital to support firm growth

projects.project_abstract: The proposed operation is part of the World Bank-financed Regional Air Quality Management (AQM) Program in the Indo-Gangetic Plain and Himalayan Foothills (IGP-HF) region, which supports Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, and Pakistan in institutional strengthening, emissions reduction, and regional knowledge exchange, forming the foundation of airshed management across the region. In India, the IGP covers around 18 percent of the country's land area and nearly 40 percent of its population, where rapid urbanization and economic growth have driven substantial emissions from transport, industry, road dust, and construction activities, making it a global air pollution hotspot. The Program aligns with India's Viksit Bharat 2047 vision, the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), India's Nationally Determined Contribution commitments, and interstate airshed directives from the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM).The CAQM estimated the source contributions through a meta-analysis of emissions inventory studies from 2015 to 2025 that were available for Delhi or data shared by a panel of experts convened by CAQM in Identification of the causes for worsening AQI in Delhi National Capital Region (NCR), Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas, January 2026 (CAQM, 2026). Delhi has implemented one of India’s most comprehensive air pollution control programs, combining policy reforms, enforcement measures, infrastructure investments, and sectoral interventions. The government’s commitment is reflected in the Delhi Air Pollution Mitigation Action Plan (DAPMP) 2026 and the allocation of a Green Budget of US$2.4 billion (21.44% of total Government of National Capital of Delhi (GNCTD) budget for FY 2026-27) for mainstreaming environmental considerations in government planning and expenditure. However, the complexity of managing emissions across sectors and jurisdictions—particularly given the transboundary nature of sources and evolving meteorological influences—requires strengthened coordination, implementation consistency, and evidence-based decision-making.DCAP Phase 1 is part of a proposed seven-year Multi-Phase Programmatic Approach (MPA), supporting the GNCTD with successive financing operations to manage the complexity of cross-sector interventions and build sustained air quality management systems. The phased approach enables sequencing—from immediate emission reduction actions to longer-term investments and structural reforms—while incorporating learning and scaling across phases.  Phase 1 of the Program would focus on: (i) short- to medium-term actions to reduce air pollution in major sources of PM2.5 emissions - transport and road dust; and (ii) development of a long-term AQM plan and its corresponding institutional framework. Subsequent phases are expected to scale and deepen these interventions and expand support to additional sectors and strengthen policy frameworks based on emerging evidence and priorities for sustained air quality improvements. DCAP Phase 1 would finance a Program for Results (PforR) combined with technical assistance to support GNCTD’s multi-sector effort across four results areas (RAs): 1)	Strengthening AQM Planning, ,Coordination and Citizen Engagement: Global experience demonstrates that a robust AQM framework is crucial to achieving sustained, measurable clean air improvements. Delhi has established an extensive policy and regulatory foundation, as well as a dense air quality monitoring network, which provide a strong platform for further consolidation. Opportunities remain to strengthen multi-sector planning, improve data quality and integration, develop more effective policies and financing instruments, update emissions inventories, and enhance monitoring, enforcement, and inter-agency coordination for enhanced implementation and enforcement of clean air initiatives. A well-designed and sustained communications and behaviour change strategy can also strengthen public awareness, encourage behavioural shifts, and foster broader stakeholder engagement. The first phase would support the GNCTD: (i) develop and start implementing a medium-term Delhi Air Pollution Management Plan (DAPMP) 2027-2031, including defined targets, budget, governance framework and M&E systems; (ii) set up the institutional arrangements of DAPMP, and (iii) design and deploy a strategic communications plan.2)	Reducing Emissions from Transport: Transport plays a significant and complex role in Delhi NCR's air quality crisis, acting as a major year-round contributor to pollution. Transport emissions account for an estimated 19–23% of primary PM2.5 concentrations and 81%  of nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions in Delhi (CAQM 2026) which is a precursor of secondary particulate matter contributing to PM2.5. Rapid and sustained growth in the vehicle fleet, coupled with significant daily traffic inflows from neighbouring NCR cities—including a high share of heavy-duty diesel vehicles (trucks and buses) that contribute disproportionately to particulate matter emissions—has intensified the problem. This is further exacerbated by the prevalence of older and poorly maintained vehicles with weak emission controls, resulting in real-world emissions that often exceed certified standards. Systematic solutions to decouple growth in transport demand from emissions, while transitioning towards cleaner vehicles, could significantly reduce transport emissions. While electrification presents a major opportunity for emission reduction, the pace of transition is constrained by gaps in charging infrastructure, including inadequate charger density, uneven spatial distribution of charging stations, limited charging options for commercial and heavy-duty vehicles, and challenges related to land availability and grid connectivity. The first phase interventions for transport sector would focus on strengthening enforcement systems, enabling conditions for scaled transition to cleaner and public transport. Key activities would include (i) enhancing enforcement mechanisms to limit entry and operation of high emitting (pre-BS VI vehicles) and end-of-life vehicles; (ii) accelerating implementation of Delhi’s upcoming EV Policy 2.0 and rollout of charging infrastructure; (iii) strengthening the electric bus (e-bus) ecosystem through bus service optimization and depot infrastructure readiness; (iv) creating an inter-agency coordination mechanism for integrated planning and delivery of mobility services in the city.3)	Reducing Emissions from Road Dust: Road dust is recognized as a major contributor to particulate pollution, particularly in dense urban environments with extensive road networks and ongoing construction activity. Emissions from soil, road and C&D dust within Delhi NCR and beyond account for 15% to 27% of primary PM2.5 concentration in Delhi in winter and summer, respectively (CAQM 2026). Delhi's road network spans an estimated 16,040 lane-km, is managed across multiple agencies with distinct mandates - including the Public Works Department (PWD), the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) and the New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC), as well as the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) and 9 other agencies.  This distributed structure requires strengthened coordination across agencies for minimizing dust generation from repeated construction activity on same streets and effective implementation of dust control measures. There is an opportunity to expand vacuum sweeping with close performance monitoring across greater share of Delhi’s road network, while strengthening coordinated planning and asset management across agencies to reduce repeated excavation and improve road conditions.Strategic Alignment to CPF. DCAP is closely aligned with the India CPF FY2026-2031 and with the vision for a Viksit Bharat 2047. The operation would address a critical challenge identified in the CPF - poor air quality - and support the CPF’s emphasis on improved livability, sustainability
projects.pdo: Strengthen air quality management (AQM) and reduce air pollutant emissions from transport in Delhi NCT
